newsitem.title: USA: US soy acres seen higher in weather-damaged areas.
newsitem.headline: US soy acres seen higher in weather-damaged areas.

text.p: U.S. soybean acreage is likely to expand in areas where severe weather has damaged crops or delayed plantings, agronomists and grain analysts said.
"I would say in some of the wheat areas that they do tear up, beans are one of the alternative crops," said Anne Frick, oilseed analyst with Prudential Securities in New York.
"Soybeans could go into Kansas and Oklahoma, as well as the Red River Valley, she said."
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's last report, 68.8 million acres of soybeans will be planted.
That acreage would be the highest since 1980, USDA said.

Analysts see acreage growth in Central Plains states where some hard red winter wheat was recently killed by freezing temperatures and in the areas where plantings have been delayed by flooding, crop observers said.
There, farmers are expected to tear up their wheat and plant either soybeans or sorghum, analysts said.
"We might see more soybean acreage in wheat states like Kansas," said Jason Roose, grain analyst with U.S. Commodities in West Des Moines, Iowa.
Farmers in North Dakota, where severe spring flooding has delayed plantings, might also put more acres into soybeans, agronomists there said.
"But they frost a little bit earlier in the Dakotas so they like to have beans in by mid-May," Roose said.

"The people in the (Red River) Valley are the ones who are going to be changing their minds because they haven't been able to put in their early season crops," said Greg Endres, extension agronomist with North Dakota State University.
In other areas of North Dakota, late-season acreage switching to soybeans is unlikely because short-maturing soybean seed stock has already been purchased, Endres said.
Some spring wheat farmers, encouraged by high soybean prices, had already planned to plant soybeans instead of spring wheat, Endres said.

Although it is much too late in the Midwest planting season to switch corn acreage to soybeans on a broad scale, high soybean prices and tight old crop soybean stocks could cause soybean acreage to creep higher, analysts said.
"In a demand bull market when you have high prices in the spring, you do tend to see the June plantings figure be above the spring intentions," Frick said.
The minimum acreage increase in analogous years is one percent, so June soybean acreage could climb up to 69.5 million acres by June, Frick said.

On Friday, old-crop July soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade scored a fresh contract high of $8.96 per bushel, and the market has recently been trading at the highest levels since the 1988 drought.
However, the new crop soybean/corn price ratio is currently 2.5 to 1.0, "which isn't "enough to cause that much (acreage) switching," Frick said.
